```{=html}
<!--
PSYCH 251 replication report template.

Every project uses this structure so that reports are comparable across the class. They
become public supplementary material, so write for a reader who has the original paper but
not your repository.

The project has two phases, and so does this report:
  Phase 1, the replication. Introduction and Methods are written, critiqued and preregistered
           BEFORE data collection; the Methods addendum, Results and Discussion after it.
  Phase 2, the extension. Proposed after Phase 1 (Rationale, Changes from Phase 1, Power and
           sample, Analysis plan), then run, with its own Results and Discussion.
The AI use statement and the Key statistics table sit at the top and are kept current
throughout. Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas for Phase 2.

Render this file at every stage. Before a phase has data, its results say so and skip
themselves; during Pilot A the Phase 1 results run on pilot data, which is the point of Pilot A.

Grey "Guidance" boxes are instructions. Delete each one once you have written that section.
The code is wired to the template's demo experiment (the framing problem). Replace the demo
specifics with your study's as you go: the experiment ids, the original study's numbers, the
exclusion rule, and the key comparison.
-->
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "galinsky2008-phase1-fullsample"
experiment_id_phase2 <- "galinsky2008-phase2"
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures.
#
# Galinsky et al. (2008), Experiment 3, Results. N = 45; 3 participants were excluded for
# suspicion, leaving 42 (hence F(3, 38) = 3.44). The outcome is the conformity index: the mean
# of the "interesting" and "enjoyable" ratings, each 1-11 (alpha = .85, following Epley &
# Gilovich, 1999). Means and SDs are as reported. The high- and low-power ns (11 and 9) are
# inferred from the one-sample tests against the bogus ratings, t(10) and t(8); the two
# baseline ns (22 in total) are not reported, so they are NA (the baselines are not plotted).
#
# The paper's high vs low test, t(38) = 2.00, used the error term from all four conditions.
# Recomputed as a two-group Student's t from these means, SDs and ns it is t(18) = -2.13.
condition_labels <- c(`1` = "High power", `2` = "Low power",
                      `3` = "Conformity baseline", `4` = "Attitude baseline")
label_condition <- function(x) factor(unname(condition_labels[as.character(x)]), levels = condition_labels)

original <- tibble(
  condition = label_condition(1:4),
  n         = c(11, 9, NA, NA),
  mean      = c(8.68, 9.55, 9.59, 8.56),
  sd        = c(1.03, 0.73, 0.77, 1.23)
)
# Mean of the ten bogus "previous participant" ratings, as reported (9.75).
bogus_mean <- 9.75
```

# Key statistics

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# A numeric column from the export, or NA if no row had that field (write order varies).
num_col <- function(df, name) if (name %in% names(df)) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[name]])) else rep(NA_real_, nrow(df))

# Suspicion is coded by hand, blind to condition (the original excluded 3 participants for
# suspicion). Each render adds any newly completed participants to suspicion_codes.csv in the
# phase's data folder: their two suspicion answers under a random code, in random order, with
# no condition and no participant id. The coder fills in `suspicious` (TRUE or FALSE) and saves
# the file; existing rows are never overwritten. suspicion_key.csv links codes to participants;
# the coder should not open it. Participants not yet coded are kept and counted.
suspicion_codes <- function(dir, trials, complete) {
  answers <- trials |>
    filter(task == "suspicion", participant_id %in% complete$participant_id) |>
    mutate(resp = map(response, ~ if (is.na(.x) || .x == "") list() else fromJSON(.x))) |>
    transmute(participant_id,
              # Early Pilot A sessions had a single placeholder question saved as `suspicion`.
              purpose = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$suspicion_purpose %||% .x$suspicion %||% "")),
              strange = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$suspicion_strange %||% "")))
  codes_path <- file.path(dir, "suspicion_codes.csv")
  key_path   <- file.path(dir, "suspicion_key.csv")
  codes <- if (file.exists(codes_path)) read_csv(codes_path, col_types = cols(.default = "c")) else
    tibble(code = character(), purpose = character(), strange = character(), suspicious = character())
  key <- if (file.exists(key_path)) read_csv(key_path, col_types = cols(.default = "c")) else
    tibble(code = character(), participant_id = character())

  new_ids <- setdiff(answers$participant_id, key$participant_id)
  if (length(new_ids) > 0) {
    used     <- as.integer(sub("^S", "", key$code))
    new_key  <- tibble(code = sprintf("S%04d", sample(setdiff(1:9999, used), length(new_ids))),
                       participant_id = sample(new_ids))
    new_rows <- new_key |> left_join(answers, by = "participant_id") |>
      transmute(code, purpose, strange, suspicious = "") |> arrange(code)
    key   <- bind_rows(key, new_key)
    # Sort the whole file by its random codes, not just the new rows, so that a later batch
    # (such as a one-condition top-up) is spread through the file instead of sitting at the
    # end, where its position would reveal its condition. Rows are matched by code, so
    # reordering never changes a code already entered.
    codes <- bind_rows(codes, new_rows) |> arrange(code)
    write_csv(key, key_path)
    write_csv(codes, codes_path, na = "")
  }
  flag <- toupper(trimws(codes$suspicious %|% ""))
  codes$suspicious <- case_when(flag %in% c("TRUE", "T", "YES", "Y", "1") ~ TRUE,
                                flag %in% c("FALSE", "F", "NO", "N", "0") ~ FALSE,
                                TRUE ~ NA)
  key |> left_join(select(codes, code, suspicious), by = "code") |> select(participant_id, suspicious)
}
`%|%` <- function(x, y) ifelse(is.na(x), y, x)

# Test runs whose Prolific ID looks real, so the "no real Prolific ID" rule in read_phase()
# cannot catch them (e.g. previewing the study on Prolific; the ID has no submission on
# Prolific). Listed per experiment id, as full participant ids (`<uid>-<run id>`).
known_test_runs <- list(`galinsky2008-pilot-b` = c("z4u4vKCKQkPyz5zG1mR1V9icrk82-86732787"))

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(participant_id = as.character(participant_id), condition = label_condition(condition))
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 1e5) |>
    mutate(participant_id = as.character(participant_id), condition = label_condition(condition))
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  # A session counts as complete only if the participant consented: declining consent ends
  # the study at once, and the saver still marks that short session completed.
  consent <- trials |> filter(task == "consent") |>
    transmute(participant_id, consented = as.logical(consented)) |>
    distinct(participant_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
  participants <- participants |> left_join(consent, by = "participant_id")

  # Test runs are not participants: sessions with no real Prolific ID (missing, or Prolific's
  # unfilled placeholder "{{%PROLIFIC_PID%}}") and the known_test_runs above. The IDs are only
  # in the gitignored identifiers.csv; just the participant ids that pass are taken from it,
  # and nothing from it is printed. Without that file (e.g. a fresh clone) only the
  # known_test_runs are left out.
  ids_path <- file.path(dir, "identifiers.csv")
  with_pid <- if (file.exists(ids_path)) {
    read_csv(ids_path, col_types = cols(.default = "c"), col_select = c(participant_id, prolific_pid)) |>
      filter(!is.na(prolific_pid), trimws(prolific_pid) != "", prolific_pid != "{{%PROLIFIC_PID%}}") |>
      pull(participant_id)
  } else {
    participants$participant_id
  }
  participants <- participants |>
    mutate(test_run = !(participant_id %in% with_pid) | participant_id %in% known_test_runs[[id]])
  # Exclusion rule, step 1: a real participant who consented and completed the study.
  complete <- participants |> filter(!test_run, completed, consented %in% TRUE)

  # Conformity index, as in the original: the mean of the "interesting" and "enjoyable"
  # ratings on the evaluation sheet (1-11). Missing if either rating was left blank.
  sheet <- trials |> filter(task == "evaluation_sheet")
  ratings <- tibble(participant_id = sheet$participant_id,
                    interesting = num_col(sheet, "interesting"),
                    enjoyable   = num_col(sheet, "enjoyable")) |>
    mutate(conformity = (interesting + enjoyable) / 2)

  susp <- suspicion_codes(dir, trials, complete)

  # Exclusion rule, step 2: not coded as suspicious. The key test then uses everyone with a
  # conformity index (both ratings given).
  checked  <- complete |> left_join(ratings, by = "participant_id") |> left_join(susp, by = "participant_id")
  keep     <- checked |> filter(!(suspicious %in% TRUE))
  analysed <- keep |> filter(!is.na(conformity))

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep, analysed = analysed,
       n_declined_consent = sum(participants$consented %in% FALSE),
       n_suspicious     = sum(checked$suspicious %in% TRUE),
       n_uncoded        = sum(is.na(checked$suspicious)),
       n_missing_rating = sum(is.na(keep$conformity)))
}

# The conditions the final study assigns (ASSIGNED_CONDITIONS in experiment.js). Tables and
# figures always show these; any other condition is shown only if someone was in it (as in
# the pilots, which also ran conditions 3 and 4), so there are no empty rows for them.
study_conditions <- label_condition(1:2)

# Conformity index by condition among analysed participants: n, mean, SD.
condition_means <- function(d) {
  d$analysed |>
    group_by(condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(conformity), sd = sd(conformity), .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(condition %in% study_conditions | n > 0)
}

# The key statistic: high power minus low power on the conformity index, with a 95% CI, from
# a Student's (equal-variance) t-test computed from the condition summaries, so the original
# and the replication go through exactly the same code. d is Cohen's d (pooled SD). NULL
# until both conditions have at least two analysed participants and some spread.
diff_ci <- function(summ) {
  hi <- summ[summ$condition == "High power", ]
  lo <- summ[summ$condition == "Low power", ]
  if (nrow(hi) == 0 || nrow(lo) == 0 || is.na(hi$n) || is.na(lo$n) || hi$n < 2 || lo$n < 2) return(NULL)
  df <- hi$n + lo$n - 2
  sp <- sqrt(((hi$n - 1) * hi$sd^2 + (lo$n - 1) * lo$sd^2) / df)
  if (!is.finite(sp) || sp == 0) return(NULL)
  se  <- sp * sqrt(1 / hi$n + 1 / lo$n)
  est <- hi$mean - lo$mean
  tibble(N = hi$n + lo$n, estimate = est,
         ci_low = est - qt(0.975, df) * se, ci_high = est + qt(0.975, df) * se,
         statistic = est / se, df = df, p = 2 * pt(-abs(est / se), df),
         d = est / sp, sd_pooled = sp)
}

# Side-by-side figure: condition means with 95% CIs for any number of studies on the same
# axes (the full 1-11 scale), in the order given. Conditions with no reported n get no bar.
study_colours <- c("#009E73", "#0072B2", "#D55E00")   # Okabe-Ito; passes the CVD checks
study_shapes  <- c(16, 17, 15)
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    filter(is.na(n) | n > 0) |>
    mutate(half  = ifelse(!is.na(n) & n > 1, qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * sd / sqrt(n), NA_real_),
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           label = ifelse(is.na(n), "n = ?", sprintf("n = %d", n)))
  # Show only the study conditions (high and low power); baselines are left out for every study.
  df <- df |> filter(condition %in% study_conditions) |> mutate(condition = droplevels(condition))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.6)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = mean, colour = Study, shape = Study)) +
    # The mean of the bogus ratings on the feedback sheet (explained in the figure caption).
    geom_hline(yintercept = bogus_mean, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - half, ymax = mean + half), position = dodge, width = 0.2,
                  linewidth = 0.6, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_point(position = dodge, size = 3) +
    geom_text(aes(y = 1.4, label = label), position = dodge, size = 2.8, colour = "grey30",
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    # Clip the view, not the data, so a wide interval is cut at the axis instead of dropped.
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:11) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 11)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(study_colours[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = setNames(study_shapes[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Conformity index (1–11)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r, collected = FALSE) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "",
                  `Difference (high − low)` = if (collected) "too few analysed participants to compute" else "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", t = "", p = "", d = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", as.integer(r$df), r$statistic),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
         d = sprintf("%.2f", r$d))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", diff_ci(original)),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) diff_ci(condition_means(phase1)), collected = have_data),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) diff_ci(condition_means(phase2)), collected = have_phase2)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllrr",
               caption = "Key comparison: conformity index (mean of the interesting and enjoyable ratings, 1–11), high-power minus low-power condition, Student's t-test. N counts the two conditions compared. The original row is recomputed from the reported means, SDs and ns; the paper's own test, t(38) = 2.00 (p ≈ .05), used the error term from all four conditions.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

I am broadly interested in how children understand social hierarchy, particularly how they reason about power, merit, and legitimacy. For this project, I have selected a related paper that explores whether power protects people from being influenced. I chose this paper because this adult study is a useful starting point in regards to understanding how people come to understand social structures involving power.

The stimuli used in this study were a sentence formation task, autobiographical power-priming instructions, and (bogus) previous participation evaluation sheets. The key statistical test that I preregistered was an independent-samples t-test comparing the conformity means of the high-power and low-power conditions. Since the original study was done in-person, one challenge I might face is replicating the conformity manipulation, since it relies on deception. Online participants might be more skeptical of bots, especially with the bogus evaluation sheets. One rescue measure I could take would be to come up with a cover story to make this more convincing for participants.

## Methods

### Power analysis

The original paper did not report an effect size, so I calculated it from the statistics reported from this experiment. I calculated that the original effect size was 0.96 (calculated from the high power condition(M = 8.68, SD = 1.03, n = 11) and the low power condition M = 9.55, SD = 0.73, n = 9)). For a two-sided independent sample t-test with α = .05, detecting this effect required 19, 24, and 30 participants per group for 80%, 90%, and 95% power, respectively. As this original effect could have been overestimated, I based the planned sample size on d =0.72, which meant that the original groups would have had to detect approximately 33% power. A power analysis indicated that 32 participants per group would provide 80% power to detect this effect, so I plan to have 32 participants in each of the high and low power conditions with bogus evaluation sheets (64 across both conditions).\
Assuming that some participants (about 15% estimated) will be excluded due to suspicions about the experiments (as in the original study), or incomplete ratings, I divided 32 by 0.85 for a recruitment target of 38 participants per condition, or 76 in total. At 8.12 dollars per hour and an estimated completion time of 11 minutes, I budgeted paying \~1.49/ participant (approximately \$151 total for participants).

```{r}
#| label: power
orig_stats <- diff_ci(original)
original_d <- abs(orig_stats$d)

# Power of a two-sided, two-sample Student's t-test with group sizes n1 and n2 at effect size d
# (base R, noncentral t; equal group sizes give the same answer as power.t.test).
power_two_sample <- function(d, n1, n2, alpha = 0.05) {
  df  <- n1 + n2 - 2
  ncp <- d * sqrt(n1 * n2 / (n1 + n2))
  tc  <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df)
  pt(tc, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE) + pt(-tc, df, ncp = ncp)
}

# d33 (Simonsohn, 2015): the effect size the original study had 33% power to detect, with its
# high- and low-power group sizes (11 and 9), alpha = .05 two-sided.
n_orig_high <- original$n[original$condition == "High power"]
n_orig_low  <- original$n[original$condition == "Low power"]
d33 <- uniroot(function(d) power_two_sample(d, n_orig_high, n_orig_low) - 0.33,
               interval = c(0.01, 5), tol = 1e-10)$root

effect_sizes <- c(Original = original_d, d33 = d33)
power_rows <- map_dfr(names(effect_sizes), function(es) {
  map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
    n <- power.t.test(delta = effect_sizes[[es]], sd = 1, power = pw, sig.level = 0.05)$n
    tibble(effect = sprintf("%s (d = %.2f)", es, effect_sizes[[es]]),
           power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n), n_total = 2 * ceiling(n))
  })
})

# 2.5 times the original high- and low-power samples (11 and 9).
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$n[1:2])

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Effect size", "Power", "N per condition", "N total (2 conditions)"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original high- vs low-power difference (%.2f points, d = %.2f) and d33 (d = %.2f, the effect the original's 11 vs 9 design had 33%% power to detect), Student's t-test, two-sided alpha = .05. The total assumes equal allocation to both conditions.",
               orig_stats$estimate, original_d, d33))

# Planned sample: 80% power at d33, inflated for expected exclusions.
n_analysed            <- power_rows$n_per_group[power_rows$effect == sprintf("d33 (d = %.2f)", d33) &
                                                power_rows$power == "80%"]
expected_exclusion_rate <- 0.15
n_recruit_per_group   <- ceiling(n_analysed / (1 - expected_exclusion_rate))

# Cost of the two key conditions on Prolific. fee_rate is Prolific's service fee as a share of
# the reward: check the current rate on Prolific's pricing page and edit it here.
reward_per_hour  <- 8
study_minutes    <- 11
fee_rate         <- 1 / 3
reward_per_participant <- round(reward_per_hour * study_minutes / 60, 2)
cost_per_participant   <- reward_per_participant * (1 + fee_rate)
n_recruit_key          <- 2 * n_recruit_per_group
total_cost_key         <- n_recruit_key * cost_per_participant

planned <- tribble(
  ~Quantity, ~Value,
  "Original d (high vs low)",                          sprintf("%.4f", original_d),
  "Original group sizes (high, low)",                  sprintf("%d, %d", n_orig_high, n_orig_low),
  "d33",                                               sprintf("%.4f", d33),
  "Power of the original design at d33 (check)",       sprintf("%.4f", power_two_sample(d33, n_orig_high, n_orig_low)),
  "Planned analysed n per group (80% power at d33)",   as.character(n_analysed),
  "Expected exclusion rate",                           sprintf("%.2f", expected_exclusion_rate),
  "n to recruit per group",                            as.character(n_recruit_per_group),
  "n to recruit, two key conditions",                  as.character(n_recruit_key),
  "Reward per hour",                                   sprintf("$%.2f", reward_per_hour),
  "Study length (minutes)",                            as.character(study_minutes),
  "Reward per participant",                            sprintf("$%.2f", reward_per_participant),
  "Fee rate",                                          sprintf("%.4f", fee_rate),
  "Cost per participant (reward + fee)",               sprintf("$%.2f", cost_per_participant),
  "Total cost, two key conditions",                    sprintf("$%.2f", total_cost_key)
)
knitr::kable(planned, align = "lr",
             caption = "Planned sample and cost, two key conditions (high and low power). Edit expected_exclusion_rate, reward_per_hour, study_minutes and fee_rate in this chunk.")
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half[1]` in the high-power condition and `r two_and_half[2]` in the low-power condition (`r sum(two_and_half)` in total).

### Planned sample

The planned sample is US residents on Prolific, who are fluent in English, and aged 18 or older. Data will be collected until each key condition has 32 people who pass the exclusions.

### Materials

### Power Prime

The first task participants completed comprised the power manipulation, which was identical to the procedure used by Galinsky et al. (2003). Participants were asked to recall and write about a particular incident in their lives and\were given a sheet of paper with 19 lines to complete this task.Those participants assigned to the high-power condition were instructed:

"Recall a particular incident in which you had power over another individual or individuals. By power, we mean a situation in which you controlled the ability of another person or persons to get something they wanted, or were in a position to evaluate those individuals. Please describe this situation in which you had power—what happened, how you felt, etc”

Those participants assigned to the low-power condition were instructed,

"Please recall a particular incident in which someone else had power over you. By power, we mean a situation in which someone had control over your ability to get something you wanted, or was in a position to evaluate you. Please describe this situation in which you did not have power—what happened, how you felt, etc.”

The power priming instructions were followed precisely in this replication.

Link to study: https://psych251.github.io/galinsky2008/

Evaluation Sheet The feedback sheet ratings, comments, title, and directions were followed precisely in this replication.

Other

Conditions 1 and 2 of the original study were followed, in addition to the task format, outcome (ratings), and the suspicion inclusion.

### Procedure

Before the study starts: Participants access the study though a Prolific link. They must be on a desktop or laptop (phones and tablets are turned away before consent). Participants are randomly assigned to a cognition when the experiment loads. They are unaware of what condition they are in. The conditions are as follows:

1.  High-power condition, bogus evaluation sheet: asked about a time where power over another individual or individuals, saw bogus evaluation sheet of “previous participants” responses
2.  Low-power condition, bogus evaluation sheet: asked about a time where someone else had power over them, saw evaluation sheet

After the study starts: First, participants see the online consent form. If they chose to participate, they proceed through the following: In conditions 1 or 2 only), participants typed a response to the autobiographical power priming question (200 character minimum recommended), and had an option to decline. They next saw a screen that explained that they were being asked to complete a sentence formation task for a pilot study looking at “psycholinguistic decision-making processes”. Participants completed 20 of these puzzles, and were shown 5 worlds on the screen and were asked to make a sentence with 4 of them (they could skip any individual prompt). At the end of the study, participants saw a bogus participation evaluation sheet, which showed ten previous participants’ ratings and four comments, with the participant’s own row labeled 29 (in both conditions).The next screen screened for suspicion, and asked participants to type responses to these questions: Next, participants completed a short demographic questionnaire and viewed the debrief form to complete the study. The estimated time to completion is around 11 minutes.

Link to study: https://psych251.github.io/galinsky2008/

### Analysis plan

The original study computed a conformity index, the mean of how enjoyable & interesting the task was to participants, 1-11 ((α = .85). It reported t(38) using the error term from all 4 conditions as the key statistic. The authors did not state if they excluded participants for completion or missing consent, but they did state that they excluded 3 participants due to suspicion from the debriefing interview. It was unclear if participants in the in-person study opted out of the experiment. No covariates or effect sizes were reported, and only the high and low power condition n’s were inferable (11 and 9). For the analysis plan for this replication, I kept the conformity index the same as it was done in the paper. I chose to drop missing ratings from the test if either was blank but this was not reported by the authors. I pre-registered the key statistical test as an independent samples two-group t-test, high vs low (df = n₁ + n₂ − 2). To comply with the student-guide.md, I excluded participants with missing consent and incomplete studies, and also excluded participants due to suspicion in alignment with the previous study. The suspicion exclusions were done via a free response question at the end of the study, which were coded blind to the condition. In alignment with the student-guide.md, I made declining the power priming essay an option that is reported instead of grounds to exclude a participant.

**Key analysis of interest.** High powered participants in the feedback sheet condition will rate the task less favorably compared to participants in the low-power in the feedback sheet condition, tested with a two-sided independent sample t-test with α = .05 comparing the conformity indices (the mean of participants’ ratings of how interesting they thought the task was) between participants in the high and low powered conditions. The effect size is the difference in ratings (high-low), with a 95% confidence interval.

**Exclusions.** Participants were excluded due suspicions about the experiments, incomplete ratings, and not completing the study.

### Pilot B

5 participants started the study, 4 people completed it, and 1 dropped out. 

The median completion time was 8.02 minutes (min = 6.24 mins, max = 12.98 mins). For the full sample, the 11-minute estimate and the reward stay  the same to cover slower first- time participants.

In pilot B, one participant started and completed the high power condition (condition 1)  and  two participants started but only one completed the low power condition (condition 2). The participant that did not finish in condition 2 completed their consent form, saw the welcome screen, and the essay prompt. They did not reach any later tasks after declining the essay (however, there is an option to continue after declining to respond, so it is unclear why they left the study).

Two participants started and completed the conformity baseline condition, and no participants were assigned to the attitude baseline condition (This is not surprising to see for at least one condition since only 5 people started the study).  

One of the three people in conditions 1 & 2 declined to complete the essay. The participant assigned to condition 1 wrote a 500 character response to the power prime, and the participant assigned to condition 2 wrote a 228 character response to the prompt. No included participants declined to complete the sentence task - every response was at least 4 words long. 

I excluded 3 participant sessions in pilot B. After double checking the ‘participants’ and ‘identifiers’ csv files, one of these sessions  was mine after previewing the study on Prolific. Another was an unsaved session (no real Prolific ID attached) and the last was a placeholder Prolific ID. 

None of the 4 participants who completed the study were coded as suspicious. All 4 saw the feedback sheet (conditions 1-3), so they were eligible to doubt it.

The original study did not have a comprehension check (this replication also did not), only a suspicion check. Instead, as informal evidence that participants understood the tasks, I checked for essay completeness if participants were assigned to that condition, and also for a lack of declines in the sentence formation task. The essay opt-out was offered deliberately, as the consent form states participants are allowed to skip questions. One person declined to respond to this, and it does not show they misunderstood the prompt (it is unclear why they left the study) 

Before launching pilot B, I made several changes to the study. I bolded the word ‘four’ in the instructions of the sentence formation task to address a TA’s feedback in an earlier milestone. I also lso changed the device check (one Android got past this and crashed).

### Changes after Pilot B

After pilot B,I dropped the two baseline conditions so that the final study has only high-power and low-power with the feedback sheet. Participants are only assigned to conditions 1 and 2, and the robot test was updated to reflect this. I coded the pilot B answers before a coding rule was finalized, and none of the responses were suspicious/borderline.  I clarified the coding rule before preregistration (changes before this are allowed, and this narrower coding rule gives the same result). The finalized rule is below: 

- A response is marked as ‘suspicious’ if the participant says or implies that the previous ratings or comments were fake, made up, planted, or not from other real people. Responses are coded as ‘not suspicious’ if the participant only comments about high ratings, or that the task seemed boring or odd, or guesses about the study’s topic. This rule applies to conditions 1 to 3 (condition 4 has no evaluation sheet). 

- Doubtful/ambiguous answers are not coded as suspicious unless they clearly question the feedback’s sheet’s authenticity.

- The original study only mentioned that three participants were excluded for questioning the feedback sheet’s authenticity. For the above rule, I used the original paper’s criterion and added the word ‘clearly’ to rule out gray cases. 

The code in the report (power table total, figures, and flow table) was updated to include the two conditions. The flow table and corresponding sentence filter out my three test runs of the study.The participant-facing text remains the same after pilot B.

#### Deviations from the preregistered plan

### Data preparation

I coded the suspicion answers by hand according to the coding rule, without knowledge of the participants’ condition. 1 person was coded as suspicious and excluded. 4 participants left the “interesting” or “enjoyable” rating blank. As a result, they have no conformity index and were not included in the key analysis test. I removed my own preview session in Firebase, and Claude Code found no other test sessions. The 13 extra participants that were recruited for the low-power condition were analyzed with the first batch of participants according to the OSF update.

### Low-power top up

Random assignment gave 61 high-power sessions vs 34 low-power sessions by chance (two-sided binomial p=.007), leaving 48 and 25 analyzed in each group, respectively. I filed an OSF update before collecting more data, and added 13 places to the Prolific study to recruit more participants into the low-power condition. This is a deviation because these participants were not randomly assigned and were recruited about a day later. The confirmatory test pools participants from the top-up and the first round of data collection, as the OSF update stated.

### Condition switchers

In phase 1, each reload of experiment webpage randomly assigned participants to a new condition. 7 participants abandoned a session and then completed a new one, and 4 analyzed participants saw both primes as a result of this. This is a deviation because the preregistration did not cover repeat session, and these participants were not excluded. Each person was still counted once using the session they completed. See the exploratory table for information on how this impacted analyses.

### Essay decliners

The preregistration was inconsistent with what to do with participants that declined to respond to the power primes. The analysis plan stated that decliners are reported (kept), but the differences table and power paragraph said these participants would be excluded. I followed the analysis plan and the registered analysis code, which kept them (5 decliners: 3 high power, 2 low-power, all included in 85 analyzed). I also fixed two inconsistent lines in the report.

### Sample size. vs plan

The analysis plan stated that data would be collected until each condition has 32 people after exclusions, recruiting 38/condition. I ended up with 48 participants in the high-power condition and 37 in the low-power condition due to reasons specified above for the top-up solution.

## Results

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
summ <- condition_means(phase1)
summ |>
  transmute(Condition = condition, n,
            Mean = sprintf("%.2f", mean), SD = sprintf("%.2f", sd)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Conformity index (1–11) by condition, analysed participants.")

key_data <- analysed |>
  filter(condition %in% c("High power", "Low power")) |>
  mutate(condition = droplevels(condition))

# Same gate as diff_ci(): two or more per group and some spread within groups (a pooled SD of
# zero would make t.test() stop with "data are essentially constant").
if (!is.null(diff_ci(summ))) {
  # Preregistered key test: Student's independent-samples t-test, high vs low power.
  print(t.test(conformity ~ condition, data = key_data, var.equal = TRUE))
  # Robustness check, not the key test: Welch's t-test, which does not assume equal variances.
  # Preregistered (commit f994e78) alongside the key test.
  print(t.test(conformity ~ condition, data = key_data))
} else {
  key_n <- summ |> filter(condition %in% c("High power", "Low power"))
  # cat(), not message(): with `warning: false` in the header, Quarto hides message() output.
  cat("t-test not run: it needs at least two analysed participants in each of the high- and ",
      "low-power conditions, with some spread in ratings within them. So far: ",
      paste(key_n$condition, key_n$n, sep = ": ", collapse = ", "),
      "; with pilot data this is expected.\n", sep = "")
}
```

### Replication assessment

The preregistered, pooled Student's t-test of 85 analyzed participants (difference between the high and low power groups)was +0.60, 95% CI \[−0.14, 1.35\], d= 0.35. Since the CI includes 0, we cannot rule out that power had no effect on participant’s ratings (a tiny effect in the predicted direction, or an effect in the opposite direction, is still possible). The CI also excluded the original paper’s difference of -0.87 (d= -0.96, recomputed), so the data here do not fit an effect this large in the predicted direction.

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- diff_ci(original)
rep  <- diff_ci(summ)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              d = sprintf("%.2f", d),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: difference in the conformity index, high power minus low power (scale points), with Cohen's d. The original row is recomputed as a two-group test from the reported means, SDs and ns; the paper's own test, t(38) = 2.00 (p ≈ .05), used the error term from all four conditions and is slightly weaker.")
} else {
  cat("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants in each of the high- and low-power conditions.\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Conformity index (mean of the interesting and enjoyable ratings, 1–11) by condition, original study (Galinsky et al., 2008, Experiment 3, reported means and SDs) and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line is the mean of the bogus ratings shown on the feedback sheet. The original n's (11 high, 9 low) were not reported, they were inferred from the degrees of freedom from the paper's one-sample t-tests."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
comparison_plot(Original = original, `Phase 1: replication` = summ)
```

### Exploratory analyses

The exploratory analyses below explored what happened to the results if participants that elected to skip any questions were excluded from analysis.

Among the randomly assigned participants only, the difference was +1.02, 95% CI \[0.17, 1.88\], p =.020. This result suggests a significant effect in the opposite direction from the original experiment. The rank-based test gives p= .052, and dropping the one lowest low-power score (a rating of 1) makes the difference non-significant (+0.71, p= .062). Additionally, excluding the 4 participants who switches conditions does not change the result (+0.64, p=.104)This finding is not strong evidence for a reversal.

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-checks
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory: internal consistency of the two ratings (the original reported alpha = .85).
# The opt-out counts are reported under Actual sample.
both <- analysed |> select(interesting, enjoyable)
if (nrow(both) >= 3 && all(map_dbl(both, sd) > 0)) {
  item_var  <- sum(map_dbl(both, var))
  total_var <- var(both$interesting + both$enjoyable)
  cat(sprintf("Cronbach's alpha for the two ratings: %.2f (original: .85), r = %.2f, n = %d.\n",
              2 * (1 - item_var / total_var), cor(both$interesting, both$enjoyable), nrow(both)))
} else {
  cat("Alpha not computed yet: needs at least three analysed participants with varied ratings.\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-skippers
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory, not preregistered: the key test again without participants who skipped a
# question, since declining was reported rather than an exclusion. "Skipped" is (a) declined
# the essay or any sentence, or (b) that, or left age, gender or first language unanswered
# (or chose "Prefer not to say"). A blank or declined rating is already excluded from every row.
skipped <- trials |>
  filter(participant_id %in% analysed$participant_id) |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(
    opted_out = any(as.logical(declined[task %in% c("power_prime", "sentence_formation")]) %in% TRUE),
    demo_resp = list(fromJSON(response[task == "demographics"][1] %||% "{}")),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(demo_skipped = map_lgl(demo_resp, function(r) {
    blank <- function(v) is.null(v) || length(v) == 0 || is.na(v[1]) || identical(as.character(v[1]), "")
    blank(r$age) || blank(r$gender) || identical(as.character(r$gender), "none") || blank(r$native_english)
  }))
sens <- analysed |> left_join(skipped, by = "participant_id")

# The low-power top-up (see Deviations): while ASSIGNED_CONDITIONS was [2] (commit cc65933,
# pushed 2026-11-03 05:10 UTC, until commit ec4c616, pushed 06:08 UTC), every session was low
# power, so those sessions were not randomly assigned. Listed per experiment id.
topup_windows <- list(`galinsky2008-phase1-fullsample` = c("2026-11-03 05:10:03", "2026-11-03 06:08:51"))
topup <- topup_windows[[experiment_id]]
sens <- sens |>
  mutate(started = as.POSIXct(started_at, tz = "UTC"),
         in_topup = !is.null(topup) & started >= as.POSIXct(topup[1], tz = "UTC") &
                    started <= as.POSIXct(topup[2], tz = "UTC"))

# Reloading the page draws a new condition, so someone who abandoned a session and started
# again may have seen both primes. Such "switchers" share a Prolific ID with an earlier session
# assigned the other condition. The IDs are only in the gitignored identifiers.csv; nothing
# from it is printed, and without it this row is skipped.
ids_path <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", experiment_id, "identifiers.csv")
have_ids <- file.exists(ids_path)
if (have_ids) {
  pid <- read_csv(ids_path, col_types = cols(.default = "c"), col_select = c(participant_id, prolific_pid))
  other_conditions <- participants |>
    filter(!is.na(condition)) |>
    left_join(pid, by = "participant_id") |>
    filter(!is.na(prolific_pid)) |>
    select(prolific_pid, other_id = participant_id, other_condition = condition)
  switchers <- sens |>
    left_join(pid, by = "participant_id") |>
    inner_join(other_conditions, by = "prolific_pid", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    filter(other_id != participant_id, other_condition != condition) |>
    distinct(participant_id) |>
    pull(participant_id)
  sens <- sens |> mutate(switched = participant_id %in% switchers)
}

rows <- c(list(
  `All analysed (preregistered)`                      = sens,
  `Without essay or sentence opt-outs`                = sens |> filter(!opted_out),
  `Without anyone who skipped any question`           = sens |> filter(!opted_out, !demo_skipped)),
  if (!is.null(topup)) list(`Randomly assigned only (without the low-power top-up)` = sens |> filter(!in_topup)),
  if (have_ids) list(`Without participants who switched condition on a reload` = sens |> filter(!switched))
)
res <- imap_dfr(rows, function(d, name) {
  s <- d |> filter(condition %in% study_conditions) |>
    group_by(condition) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(conformity), sd = sd(conformity), .groups = "drop")
  k <- diff_ci(s)
  if (is.null(k)) return(NULL)
  tibble(Sample = name,
         `n (high / low)` = paste(s$n, collapse = " / "),
         `Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", k$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", k$ci_low, k$ci_high),
         t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", as.integer(k$df), k$statistic),
         p = if (k$p < 0.001) "< .001" else sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", k$p)),
         d = sprintf("%.2f", k$d))
})
if (nrow(res) > 0) {
  knitr::kable(res, caption = "Exploratory: the key test on different subsets of the analysed sample (Student's t, high minus low power): without participants who skipped a question, without the low-power top-up (not randomly assigned), and without participants who were assigned the other condition in an earlier, abandoned session. Not preregistered; the first row is the confirmatory result.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-outliers
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory, not preregistered: how much the key result depends on a few extreme ratings.
# (1) A rank-based test (Wilcoxon rank-sum), which does not use the size of extreme values.
# (2) The key test after dropping the k lowest conformity scores in the low-power condition,
#     where the lowest ratings are; an influence check, not an exclusion rule.
# Each check is run on all analysed participants (the preregistered sample) and on the randomly
# assigned participants only (without the low-power top-up; see exploratory-skippers above).
fmt_p3 <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< .001" else sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p))
key_all <- sens |> filter(condition %in% c("High power", "Low power")) |> mutate(condition = droplevels(condition))
samples <- c(list(`All analysed (preregistered)` = key_all),
             if (!is.null(topup)) list(`Randomly assigned only` = key_all |> filter(!in_topup)))
samples <- keep(samples, function(d) n_distinct(d$condition) == 2 && all(table(d$condition) >= 5))

# Two separate `if`s, not one block: knitr prints only a block's last table.
if (length(samples) > 0) {
  imap_dfr(samples, function(d, name) {
    w <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(conformity ~ condition, data = d))
    s <- d |> group_by(condition) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(conformity), sd = sd(conformity), .groups = "drop")
    tibble(Sample = name, `n (high / low)` = paste(s$n, collapse = " / "),
           `Student's t: p` = fmt_p3(diff_ci(s)$p),
           `Wilcoxon rank-sum: W` = sprintf("%.0f", w$statistic), `Wilcoxon: p` = fmt_p3(w$p.value))
  }) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: a rank-based test (Wilcoxon rank-sum, high vs low power) beside the Student's t-test, which does not use the size of extreme scores. Not preregistered.")
}
if (length(samples) > 0) {
  imap_dfr(samples, function(d, name) {
    low_sorted <- d |> filter(condition == "Low power") |> arrange(conformity)
    map_dfr(0:4, function(k) {
      dd <- bind_rows(d |> filter(condition == "High power"), if (k == 0) low_sorted else low_sorted |> slice(-(1:k)))
      s <- dd |> group_by(condition) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(conformity), sd = sd(conformity), .groups = "drop")
      r <- diff_ci(s)
      tibble(Sample = name, `Lowest low-power scores dropped` = k,
             `n (high / low)` = paste(s$n, collapse = " / "),
             `Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate),
             `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
             p = fmt_p3(r$p))
    })
  }) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: the key test after dropping the k lowest conformity scores in the low-power condition (k = 0 is the full sample). Not preregistered; shows how much the difference rests on a few low ratings.")
}
```

## Discussion

### Summary of replication attempt

The original finding did not replicate. The preregistered, pooled Student's t-test found a difference in the opposite direction from the original study. This difference was not significant. The original study's difference in means was -0.87, and was not within the interval of this replication attempt. The subset of participants that were randomly assigned hinted at a reversal of the original effect, but this did not hold up - it depended on a few low ratings and was not robust to a rank-based test. See the "Replication assessment" section for the preregistered test, and the "Exploratory analyses" section for the robustness checks.

### Commentary

Overall, the online power prime might not have made people feel powerful/powerless. Online participants might have also not believed the bogus evaluation sheet. Phase 2 will address the aforementioned issues as plausible reasons for the failure.

# Phase 2: Extension

**Track:** Best-practices rescue

# Rationale

There are two plausible reasons that Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result. Firstly, it is possible that the typed, online power prime may not have made people feel powerful or powerless - phase 1 had no way to check. Adding a manipulation check tests whether the prime changed how powerful people felt. Secondly, it is possible that participants did not believe the bogus sheet. A funnel debrief would get at this directly by asking whether people noticed and believed the sheet.\

## Power and sample

The original study found participants in the high-power condition rated the task about 0.87 points lower. With 62 people per condition in phase 2, this effect can be detected 80% of the time. I plan to recruit 73 per group (146 total) to account for exclusions/dropouts. At a rate of 8.12/hour with a slightly longer study (\~14 mins), this would cost \~\$369 (including platform fees). 

I added after the ratings so that phase 2 result is directly comparable to phase 1. With more people, the range of possible results becomes narrower: ±0.61 (instead of ±0.74 from phase 1). 

One limitation of this plan is that 62 analyzed participants is enough to catch an effect as large as the original’s - it is not enough to reliably catch a small effect.  

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n_per_group <- 62    # planned analysed participants per condition in Phase 2

p1_stats <- if (have_data) diff_ci(condition_means(phase1))
orig_stats <- diff_ci(original)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(delta = p1_stats$estimate, sd = p1_stats$sd_pooled, source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(delta = orig_stats$estimate, sd = orig_stats$sd_pooled, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the high - low difference at n per condition.
half_width <- function(n) qt(0.975, 2 * n - 2) * basis$sd * sqrt(2 / n)
power_at <- function(n, delta, sd) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = abs(delta), sd = sd, sig.level = 0.05)$power, error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed (high + low)` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, 2 * phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.2f points", (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.2f points (expected)", half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.2f points", orig_stats$estimate),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.2f points", p1_stats$estimate),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.2f points", orig_stats$estimate / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, orig_stats$estimate, basis$sd),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, p1_stats$estimate, basis$sd),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, orig_stats$estimate / 2, basis$sd)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test at %d per condition, Student's t, two-sided alpha = .05, assuming an SD of %.2f (from %s).",
                                 phase2_n_per_group, basis$sd, basis$source))
```

## Analysis plan

The key analysis test for phase 2 will be kept identical to phase 1: a two sided Student’s t-test comparing high vs low power on the conformity index. This will be run with data only from phase 2, with α = .05. I will report the difference (high -low) with its  95% CI and d. 

The exclusion rule will be kept the same from phase 1: participants will be excluded if they did not consent, did not complete the study, are coded as suspicious, and are missing any ratings. Essay decliners are kept and reported. The additional manipulation check and funnel debrief questions will not be used as grounds to exclude participants. I plan to use the manipulation check as a diagnostic to compare high vs low power participants responses to the check question. It will be analyzed separately, and never as a control variable in the main test.  Additionally, I plan to report how many people said they notice the bogus evaluation sheet. The first two open-ended questions of the debrief will remain the same as in phase 1, with the following closed format additions: 

Q3: DId you notice the other participants’ ratings? 

Answer choice: yes/no 

Q4: How much did the ratings influence yours?

Answer choice: likert scale from 1-5 (1= none at all, 5= a great deal) 

Q5: How much did you  believe those ratings came from real previous participants?

Answer choice: likert scale from 1-5 (1= not at all, 5= a great deal) 

For Q4, I will report the average Q4 score (how much ratings from the bogus sheet influenced theirs, 1-5 ) separately for the high power and low power condition. Similarly for Q5, I will report the average Q5 score (how much people believed the ratings were real, 1-5) separately for each condition. I chose to calculate the mean to avoid picking an arbitrary number on the scale as a cutoff for "believed". 

\

```{r}
if (!is.null(p2_stats)) {
  tibble(`Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", p2_stats$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", p2_stats$ci_low, p2_stats$ci_high),
         t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", as.integer(p2_stats$df), p2_stats$statistic),
         p = fmt_p(p2_stats$p), d = sprintf("%.2f", p2_stats$d)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2 key test (preregistered): Student's t-test, high vs low power, conformity index.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: phase2-checks
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
# The Phase 2 checks, as in the Analysis plan, for analysed participants: the manipulation
# check (how powerful they felt while writing, 1-5, 5 = extremely) compared between conditions on its own,
# never as a control in the key test; and funnel questions 3-5 (noticed the ratings, yes/no;
# how much they influenced theirs and how much they believed them, 1-5, 5 = a great deal), by condition.
p2_trials <- phase2$trials
# A column is absent from the export if nobody answered that question; add it as missing.
for (col in c("manip_power", "funnel_noticed", "funnel_influence", "funnel_belief")) {
  if (!col %in% names(p2_trials)) p2_trials[[col]] <- NA
}
p2_checks <- p2_trials |>
  filter(participant_id %in% phase2$analysed$participant_id, task %in% c("manipulation_check", "funnel")) |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(manip_power      = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(first(na.omit(manip_power)))),
            funnel_noticed   = first(na.omit(as.character(funnel_noticed))),
            funnel_influence = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(first(na.omit(funnel_influence)))),
            funnel_belief    = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(first(na.omit(funnel_belief)))),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  right_join(phase2$analysed |> select(participant_id, condition), by = "participant_id") |>
  filter(condition %in% study_conditions) |>
  mutate(condition = droplevels(condition))
mean_sd <- function(x) if (sum(!is.na(x)) == 0) "—" else sprintf("%.2f (%.2f), n = %d", mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(x)))

# Separate `if`s, not one block: knitr prints only a block's last table.
if (nrow(p2_checks) > 0) {
  p2_checks |>
    group_by(Condition = condition) |>
    summarise(`Felt powerful (1–5), M (SD)` = mean_sd(manip_power),
              `Noticed the ratings` = sprintf("%d of %d answered", sum(funnel_noticed %in% "Yes"), sum(!is.na(funnel_noticed))),
              `Influence (1–5), M (SD)` = mean_sd(funnel_influence),
              `Believed real (1–5), M (SD)` = mean_sd(funnel_belief),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2 checks by condition, analysed participants (all 1–5 scales: 5 = extremely or a great deal). All questions were optional; n counts those who answered.")
}

# Manipulation check: high vs low power, Student's t (the prime worked if high power is higher).
manip <- p2_checks |> filter(!is.na(manip_power))
if (nrow(manip) > 0 && all(table(manip$condition) >= 2) && sd(manip$manip_power) > 0) {
  m <- t.test(manip_power ~ condition, data = manip, var.equal = TRUE)
  tibble(`Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", unname(diff(rev(m$estimate)))),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", m$conf.int[1], m$conf.int[2]),
         t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", as.integer(m$parameter), m$statistic),
         p = fmt_p(m$p.value)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2 manipulation check: how powerful participants felt while writing (1–5, 5 = extremely), high minus low power, Student's t-test. Analysed separately from the key test.")
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8

                `Phase 1: replication` = if (have_data) condition_means(phase1),
                `Phase 2: extension` = condition_means(phase2))
```
